items.description: Personally identifiable information, including Social Security numbers, policy numbers tied to individuals, dates of birth, and health details, must never appear in URL paths or query strings, where it would persist in logs, browser histories, and proxies. Such data is conveyed only in request bodies or headers over encrypted channels, with opaque identifiers used for resource addressing.

items.name: No Stack Traces in Production
items.description: Production error responses must never include stack traces, internal class names, SQL fragments, or infrastructure details. Diagnostic context is written to centralized logging with a correlation identifier that is returned to the caller, allowing support teams to trace an incident without exposing internals to consumers or attackers.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟API Standards␟API Error Handling

items.name: OAuth 2.0 and OIDC
items.description: APIs are protected with OAuth 2.0 access tokens, with OpenID Connect used for user authentication and identity propagation. Scopes are defined per business capability so a consumer authorized to read claim status cannot invoke payment or policy-change operations, and token validation is enforced at the gateway as well as in the service.

items.name: OpenAPI 3.0 Specs Required
items.description: Each API must carry a complete OpenAPI 3.0 specification covering all endpoints, schemas, security schemes, and error responses. The specification is the authoritative interface description used for design review, contract testing, and partner onboarding, and an API without one cannot pass architecture review.

items.name: P95 Latency Under 200ms
items.description: APIs must serve the 95th percentile of requests in under 200 milliseconds, measured at the gateway under representative production load. Teams track this objective in their observability dashboards, and sustained breaches trigger performance remediation work before new feature delivery, since slow APIs directly degrade quoting and claims-intake experiences.

items.name: Pagination Required for Collections
items.description: Endpoints returning collections, such as policy lists, claim histories, or billing transactions, must paginate using the standard cursor or offset conventions with documented default and maximum page sizes. Unbounded result sets are prohibited because portfolio-scale queries can return millions of rows and destabilize both provider and consumer.

items.name: Published to Developer Portal
items.description: Generated specifications are published automatically to the enterprise developer portal, where they are versioned, searchable, and paired with usage guides and sandbox access. The portal is the single discovery point for all APIs, including those consumed by agency, broker, and group-benefits integration partners.

items.name: RESTful Design
items.description: APIs follow REST conventions over HTTPS, using standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) with their defined semantics and appropriate status codes. Operations must be modeled as state transfers on resources rather than remote procedure calls, so a quote, policy, or claim is manipulated through predictable, cacheable interactions.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟API Standards␟API Design Guidelines

items.name: RFC 7807 Problem Details Format
items.description: All error responses use the RFC 7807 Problem Details structure, returning application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail, and instance members. Domain-specific extensions, such as underwriting decline reasons or claim validation failures, are added as documented extension members rather than ad hoc payloads.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟API Standards␟API Error Handling

items.name: Rate Limiting
items.description: Every exposed API enforces request rate limits at the gateway, with per-consumer quotas tuned to legitimate usage patterns. Limits protect core systems like policy administration and claims platforms from abusive traffic, runaway integrations, and denial-of-service conditions, and limit breaches return the standard 429 response with retry guidance.

items.name: Resource-Oriented
items.description: Interfaces are organized around business resources such as policies, claims, insureds, and invoices, identified by stable URIs, rather than around internal system operations. Resource boundaries should reflect the insurance domain model, keeping URLs meaningful to integrators and decoupled from the implementing system's database structure.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟API Standards␟API Design Guidelines

items.name: Twelve-Month Deprecation Policy
items.description: When a version is deprecated, it remains supported for a minimum of twelve months, during which consumers receive deprecation headers, portal notices, and direct communication through the consumer registry. Retirement before the window closes requires ARB approval and confirmation that all remaining traffic has migrated.

items.name: URI Versioning for Breaking Changes
items.description: Breaking changes are released under a new major version segment in the URI, such as /v1 to /v2, leaving the prior version operational in parallel. This allows agency systems, vendor platforms, and internal consumers to migrate on their own schedules rather than being forced into lockstep releases.

items.name: ADRs Required for Significant Decisions
items.description: Any architecturally significant decision, such as selecting a policy administration integration pattern, adopting a new platform, or departing from a reference architecture, must be documented as an ADR before implementation proceeds. Each record states the context, the options considered, the decision, and its consequences in the standard template.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Architecture Decision Records

items.name: ARB Approval Required for Major Initiatives
items.description: Initiatives that exceed defined cost, risk, or cross-domain impact thresholds, including core system replacements, new vendor platforms, and material integration programs, must present to the ARB and obtain approval before funding gates are passed. Submissions use the standard solution architecture package so reviews compare like for like.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Architecture Review Board (ARB)

items.name: Approved Patterns Documented With Examples
items.description: Each reference architecture, covering areas such as API integration, event streaming, document management, and core-system extension, is documented with its intended context, component diagram, technology choices, and at least one worked example from a real implementation. Patterns are versioned and reviewed periodically so the library reflects current platforms rather than retired ones.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Reference Architecture Library

items.name: Architecture Decision Records
items.description: Defines how significant architecture choices are captured and preserved as a durable, auditable history, so future teams understand why the enterprise's systems are shaped the way they are and avoid relitigating settled decisions.

items.name: Architecture Fitness Functions
items.description: Turns architectural standards into executable checks, so compliance with the enterprise's structural rules is verified continuously by machines rather than periodically by review meetings.

items.name: Architecture Review Board (ARB)
items.description: Establishes the enterprise's senior review forum for architectural oversight, ensuring major technology investments across P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits align with the target architecture before significant spend is committed.

items.name: Automated Tests for Architecture Compliance
items.description: Teams encode architectural rules, such as dependency direction between layers, prohibited library usage, bounded-context isolation, and latency or coupling thresholds, as automated fitness functions. These tests make the intended architecture objectively measurable instead of relying on documentation and goodwill.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Architecture Fitness Functions

items.name: Decision Log Maintained
items.description: Every ARB outcome, including approvals, conditions, deferrals, and rejections, is recorded in a maintained decision log with rationale and owners for any follow-up actions. The log is accessible to delivery teams and auditors, and conditions are tracked to closure rather than forgotten after the meeting.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Architecture Review Board (ARB)

items.name: Detailed Design Reviewed by Peers
items.description: Detailed technical designs, covering component structure, data models, integration contracts, and failure handling, are reviewed by engineers and architects from outside the authoring team before build begins. Reviewers record findings and the author must resolve or formally accept each one, creating a documented quality gate below the solution-architecture level.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Technical Design Review

items.name: Deviations Require Justification and Approval
items.description: A solution that departs from an applicable reference architecture must record the business or technical justification and obtain approval through the architecture review process before build begins. Approved deviations are logged and revisited, since each one either signals a gap the library should absorb or a debt item to be remediated.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Reference Architecture Library

items.name: Failures Block Deployment
items.description: A failing fitness function is a hard gate; the pipeline stops and the change cannot be promoted until the violation is fixed or a documented, time-boxed exception is approved by the architecture function. This ensures compliance debt cannot silently accumulate in production insurance systems.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Architecture Fitness Functions

items.name: Reference Architecture Library
items.description: Maintains the curated catalog of approved architectural patterns for the enterprise, accelerating solution design by giving teams proven starting points and keeping the technology estate coherent across business lines.

items.name: Run in CI/CD
items.description: Fitness functions execute in the continuous integration pipeline on every build, alongside unit and contract tests. Running them this early surfaces architectural erosion, like a claims service reaching directly into the policy database, at the moment it is introduced rather than during an annual review.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Architecture Fitness Functions

items.name: Security, Performance, and Operability Checklist
items.description: Each review works through the standard checklist covering security items such as authentication, authorization, and data protection for policyholder information, performance items such as expected volumes and latency budgets, and operability items such as logging, monitoring, alerting, and runbook readiness. The completed checklist is attached to the design artifact as evidence of the review.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Technical Design Review

items.name: Solution Architecture Document Required Before Development
items.description: No development effort beyond approved spikes may begin until a solution architecture document has been completed and reviewed. The document covers business context, component and integration views, data flows including any PII or PHI handling, non-functional requirements, and alignment with reference architectures, giving reviewers a full picture before code is written.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Solution Design Review

items.name: Solution Design Review
items.description: Requires that every initiative's solution architecture is documented and reviewed before development starts, preventing costly rework by catching misalignment with the enterprise's platforms, data flows, and security posture at the design stage.

items.name: Standardized Template
items.description: All solution architecture documents use the enterprise template, which prescribes the required sections, diagram notations, and sign-off matrix. A common structure lets reviewers across the architecture community assess designs efficiently and makes documents comparable across the P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits portfolios.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Solution Design Review

items.name: Status Tracked Through Lifecycle
items.description: Every ADR carries an explicit status of Proposed, Accepted, or Deprecated, updated as the decision moves through review and is eventually superseded. A deprecated record is never deleted; it references the ADR that replaced it, preserving the chain of reasoning for auditors and future architects.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Architecture Decision Records

items.name: Stored in Repo
items.description: ADRs live in version control alongside the code or platform they govern, typically in a docs/adr directory, so they are diffable, reviewable through pull requests, and discoverable by the teams doing the work. Repository storage keeps the decision history coupled to the system's evolution rather than buried in shared drives.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Architecture Decision Records

items.name: Tech Debt Logged, Prioritized, and Scheduled
items.description: Identified debt items, from outdated frameworks in policy systems to shortcut integrations and missing test coverage, are recorded in the central register with a description, affected systems, risk rating, and estimated remediation effort. Items are prioritized against business risk and scheduled into delivery plans, so each entry carries an owner and a target rather than sitting as an unbounded backlog.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Technical Debt Register

items.name: Technical Debt Register
items.description: Makes technical debt a visible, managed portfolio rather than an invisible drag, ensuring the enterprise consciously balances new capability delivery against the long-term health of its systems.

items.name: Technical Design Review
items.description: Mandates peer scrutiny of detailed designs before implementation, ensuring that component-level decisions are sound, operable, and secure rather than discovered to be flawed in production.

items.name: Twenty Percent Capacity Reserved for Debt Reduction
items.description: Delivery teams reserve roughly twenty percent of each planning increment for remediating items from the debt register. This allocation is protected during planning and tracked in increment reviews, preventing feature pressure from indefinitely deferring the maintenance that keeps quoting, claims, and billing platforms reliable.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Technical Debt Register

items.name: Weekly Cadence
items.description: The board convenes weekly with a published agenda and quorum rules, keeping review latency short enough that governance does not stall delivery. Urgent items can be triaged between sessions through a documented expedited path, with the decision ratified at the next meeting.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Governance␟Architecture Review Board (ARB)

items.name: Aggregation at the BFF Layer
items.description: Composition of data from multiple domain services, for example combining policy, billing, and claims status into a single account dashboard response, happens in the BFF rather than in the client or in core services. Domain APIs stay clean and reusable while each channel receives right-sized payloads in a single round trip.

items.name: Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)
items.description: Prescribes the pattern for tailoring API experiences to each consuming channel, keeping the carrier's web, mobile, and partner experiences fast and independently evolvable without bloating shared domain services.

items.name: Bounded Contexts Map to Teams
items.description: Each bounded context is owned end to end by a single long-lived team, and system boundaries are drawn so that a context does not span teams. Aligning ownership this way keeps models internally consistent, limits cross-team coordination on changes, and makes accountability for a domain like P&C claims or retirement servicing unambiguous.

items.name: CQRS Pattern
items.description: Defines when and how to separate command and query responsibilities in system design, allowing high-volume insurance workloads to scale reads independently of writes while preserving strong audit trails where the business demands them.

items.name: Dedicated API Layer per Client Type
items.description: Each client category, including the policyholder web portal, mobile apps, and partner or agency channels, gets its own backend-for-frontend service shaped to that channel's screens and workflows. The BFF is owned by the team building the client experience, allowing channel-specific changes such as a mobile claims-photo flow without modifying shared domain APIs.

items.name: Domain-Driven Design
items.description: Establishes domain-driven design as the enterprise's approach to modeling its business in software, keeping system boundaries, team structures, and terminology aligned with how the insurance business actually operates.

items.name: Event Sourcing Optional for Audit-Heavy Domains
items.description: Domains with intensive audit and reconstruction requirements, such as claims adjudication, policy endorsements, or financial postings, may additionally adopt event sourcing so state is derived from an immutable event log. The choice is optional and made per domain, weighing the regulatory value of a complete change history against the operational cost of event-store management and replay tooling.

items.name: Event-Driven Architecture
items.description: Sets the rules for asynchronous, event-based integration between business domains, decoupling the carrier's systems so that changes in one area propagate reliably without tight runtime dependencies.

items.name: Events for Cross-Domain Communication
items.description: When one domain needs to react to changes in another, for example billing responding to a policy issuance or analytics consuming claim status changes, the interaction is implemented through published domain events on the enterprise event backbone rather than synchronous point-to-point calls. Events follow the published schema standards and are treated as part of the producing domain's public contract.

items.name: Eventual Consistency Acceptable for Non-Financial Data
items.description: Consumers of events may lag the source of record briefly, and this eventual consistency is acceptable for non-financial data such as contact updates, document status, or dashboard aggregates. Financial movements, including premium collection, claim payments, and reserve changes, require stronger consistency guarantees and must not rely on eventually consistent projections for transactional decisions.

items.name: Gradual Cutover
items.description: Existing data and traffic are migrated in planned waves, with parallel-run validation, reconciliation checks, and rollback paths at each stage. The legacy system is decommissioned only after all functions and in-force records have been transitioned and verified, and the migration plan includes explicit exit criteria for each wave.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Patterns␟Strangler Fig Migration

items.name: Independent Deployment
items.description: Every microservice is deployable on its own, with its own pipeline, versioning, and data store access, and without coordinated releases of other services. Designs that require lockstep deployment indicate hidden coupling and fail this criterion.

items.name: Legacy Modernization via Incremental Replacement
items.description: Legacy capabilities are replaced one slice at a time, with each slice, such as a product line's quoting or a specific claims workflow, rebuilt in the target architecture behind a routing facade. The legacy system keeps running throughout, and each increment must deliver verifiable, production-ready functionality before the next begins.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Patterns␟Strangler Fig Migration

items.name: Microservices Criteria
items.description: Defines the qualifying criteria a service must meet to be built and operated as a microservice, preventing both distributed monoliths and uncontrolled service sprawl across the enterprise's platforms.

items.name: New Traffic to New System
items.description: Once a replaced capability is live, new business and new transactions are routed to the modern system while the legacy platform continues serving in-force business not yet migrated. The routing layer enforces this split deterministically, for example sending new policy issuance to the new core while renewals of unmigrated policies stay on the old one.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Patterns␟Strangler Fig Migration

items.name: Saga Pattern
items.description: Establishes the saga pattern as the standard for managing distributed transactions that span multiple services, coordinating multi-step business processes such as policy issuance or claim settlement through either choreography, where services react to each other's events, or orchestration, where a workflow engine directs the steps and their compensating actions when a stage fails.

items.name: Separate Read and Write Models for High-Scale Scenarios
items.description: Where read and write loads diverge significantly, such as claims status inquiry traffic dwarfing claim updates, or agent portfolio dashboards querying policy data at high volume, systems may maintain distinct write and read models with the read side built as optimized projections. CQRS is reserved for these demonstrated scale cases, not applied by default, because it adds synchronization and consistency complexity.

items.name: Services Under 500 Lines of Business Logic
items.description: A microservice should contain fewer than roughly 500 lines of core business logic, serving as a guardrail for scope rather than a precise quota. A service trending well beyond this size signals that it is absorbing multiple responsibilities, such as combining rating and document generation, and should be evaluated for decomposition.

items.name: Sidecar/Service Mesh
items.description: Mandates a service mesh, Istio or Linkerd, for workloads running in Kubernetes, so cross-cutting concerns including mutual TLS between services, retry and timeout policies, and traffic observability are handled uniformly by the platform's sidecar proxies rather than re-implemented inconsistently inside each insurance application service.

items.name: Single Bounded Context
items.description: Each service lives entirely within one bounded context and never straddles domain boundaries. A service may implement part of the claims context, but it must not blend claims and billing concepts in one codebase or database, keeping the domain model coherent and changes localized.

items.name: Strangler Fig Migration
items.description: Prescribes the enterprise's approach to retiring legacy systems, such as aging policy administration and claims platforms, through controlled incremental replacement instead of high-risk big-bang rewrites.

items.name: Strategic DDD for Domain Modeling
items.description: Strategic domain-driven design techniques, including context mapping and subdomain classification, are used to partition the enterprise into core, supporting, and generic domains such as underwriting, claims, billing, and distribution. This strategic view guides where to invest in custom differentiating capability versus adopting commodity solutions.

items.name: Team Ownership
items.description: Each service has exactly one owning team accountable for its full lifecycle, including build, run, on-call, and eventual decommissioning. Shared or orphaned services are not permitted; if no team can own a proposed service, it should not be created as a separate deployable.

items.name: Ubiquitous Language Enforced
items.description: Within each bounded context, the same business vocabulary is used in conversation, documentation, APIs, and code, with terms defined in the context's glossary. Concepts like insured, member, claimant, and beneficiary must mean exactly one thing inside a context, eliminating the translation errors that arise when engineers and underwriting or claims staff use words differently.

items.name: API-First Design
items.description: Establishes APIs as the primary product of every capability the enterprise builds, ensuring functionality created for one channel or business line is immediately reusable across the carrier's portals, partners, and internal systems.

items.name: All Capabilities Exposed via Well-Defined APIs
items.description: Every business capability, whether rating, eligibility, claims intake, or document retrieval, is delivered behind a versioned, documented API designed before implementation begins. No capability may be reachable only through a user interface or a private database connection, so future channels and automation can consume it without rework.

items.name: Business-Aligned Technology
items.description: Requires that every technology decision, from platform selection to integration design, be traceable to the business capabilities and outcomes it supports, so architecture investment across the P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits portfolios is justified by demonstrable value such as faster product launch, improved claims experience, or reduced operating cost rather than technical preference.

items.name: Custom Build as Last Resort
items.description: Bespoke development is undertaken only when reuse and commercial options have been formally assessed and found inadequate, typically for capabilities that differentiate the carrier, such as proprietary underwriting models or distinctive customer experiences. A decision to build is documented with the comparative analysis and carries an acknowledged commitment to fund the asset's ongoing maintenance.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Principles␟Reuse Before Buy Before Build

items.name: Data as an Asset
items.description: Declares enterprise data, including policy, claims, customer, and financial information, a strategic asset that must have a named owner and steward, defined quality and governance controls, and managed availability for analytics and operations, rather than being treated as an incidental byproduct of the applications that happen to capture it.

items.name: Design for Failure
items.description: Requires every system to assume that dependencies will fail and to degrade gracefully when they do, applying retry with backoff, circuit breakers, and defined fallback behavior so that an outage in one component, such as a third-party data provider or a downstream core system, does not cascade into the loss of quoting, claims intake, or policyholder service.

items.name: Design for Replaceability
items.description: Components are built so they can be swapped out behind stable interfaces, with vendor-specific and infrastructure concerns isolated at the edges of the system. This keeps the enterprise free to replace a rating engine, document platform, or vendor service when the business case changes, without rewriting the consumers around it.

items.name: Evaluate Commercial Solutions
items.description: If no internal capability fits, commercially available software and SaaS offerings are evaluated next against functional fit, total cost of ownership, security and regulatory compliance, and integration with the enterprise architecture. The insurance software market covers most commodity needs, so the burden of proof rests on showing that available products genuinely fall short.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Principles␟Reuse Before Buy Before Build

items.name: Internal Services Are First-Class API Consumers
items.description: Internal systems integrate through the same published APIs offered to external consumers, with no privileged back doors into databases or undocumented endpoints. Treating internal consumers identically keeps contracts honest, exercises the APIs at real volume, and guarantees that what partners receive is the same hardened interface the enterprise itself depends on.

items.name: Leverage Existing Capabilities First
items.description: Before any acquisition or build, teams must search the enterprise's existing application, API, and platform inventory for a capability that already meets the need, possibly with configuration or modest extension. Duplicating a function that exists elsewhere in the carrier, such as a second document-generation or address-validation service, requires explicit justification at architecture review.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Architecture Principles␟Reuse Before Buy Before Build

items.name: Loose Coupling
items.description: Establishes minimal interdependence as a core design principle for the enterprise's systems, so individual platforms can change, scale, or be replaced without dragging the rest of the estate along with them.

items.name: Minimize Dependencies Between Systems
items.description: Designs must keep the number and depth of inter-system dependencies as low as practical, interacting through published contracts rather than shared databases or internal implementation details. Each proposed dependency is justified during design review, since every coupling point becomes a constraint on future change to core insurance platforms.

items.name: Reuse Before Buy Before Build
items.description: Defines the mandatory evaluation order for sourcing any new capability, steering investment toward the enterprise's existing assets and the commercial market before committing to custom development, and reserving engineering capacity for genuinely differentiating insurance capabilities.

items.name: Use Event-Driven Patterns
items.description: Where systems need awareness of each other's state changes, asynchronous events are preferred over synchronous request chains. Publishing events such as PolicyIssued or ClaimClosed lets consumers subscribe without the producer knowing they exist, removing temporal coupling and protecting upstream systems from downstream outages.

items.name: Auto-Scaling Configured
items.description: Production services must be configured with auto-scaling policies that absorb predictable peaks, such as open enrollment, renewal cycles, and catastrophe-driven claims surges, without manual intervention. Scaling thresholds and limits are documented and tuned based on observed load.

items.name: Cost Management
items.description: Governs how cloud spend is attributed, monitored, and optimized across ABC Insurance Group's subscriptions, ensuring every workload's cost is traceable to a business owner and that the architecture function can demonstrate ongoing efficiency to finance.

items.name: Disaster Recovery
items.description: Establishes the disaster recovery posture for cloud-hosted systems so that the carrier can continue issuing policies, paying claims, and meeting regulatory obligations after a regional outage or major failure event.

items.name: Documented DR Strategy (Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Active-Active)
items.description: Each production application must declare and document one of the approved recovery patterns: Pilot Light, Warm Standby, or Active-Active, matched to its business criticality tier. The selected pattern, failover procedure, and dependencies are recorded in the architecture repository and approved at solution design review.

items.name: Drift Detection Enabled
items.description: Automated drift detection runs against all managed environments to surface divergence between deployed resources and their declared definitions. Detected drift is triaged, and unauthorized changes are either reverted or formally incorporated into code with review.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Cloud Architecture␟Infrastructure as Code

items.name: GitOps Workflow
items.description: All infrastructure changes flow through version-controlled repositories with peer-reviewed pull requests and pipeline-driven deployment. The Git history serves as the change record for audit and incident forensics, and only the pipeline identity holds write access to managed environments.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Cloud Architecture␟Infrastructure as Code

items.name: High Availability
items.description: Defines the resilience baseline for production systems so that customer-facing and core insurance operations remain available through infrastructure failures and demand spikes, with recovery expectations agreed in advance with the business.

items.name: Hub-Spoke Topology
items.description: Cloud networks follow a hub-spoke design in which shared services, inspection, and hybrid connectivity reside in central hubs and application workloads occupy isolated spokes. Spoke-to-spoke traffic transits the hub so it can be inspected and controlled.

items.name: Identity Integration
items.description: Every landing zone is integrated with the enterprise identity provider at provisioning time, with role-based access granted through standard groups and privileged access managed via just-in-time elevation. Local or standalone identity stores are not permitted.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Cloud Architecture␟Landing Zone Standards

items.name: Infrastructure as Code
items.description: Requires that all cloud infrastructure be defined, changed, and audited through code so environments are reproducible, reviewable, and free of undocumented configuration, supporting both operational reliability and audit evidence for regulators.

items.name: Landing Zone Standards
items.description: Defines the enterprise landing zone that every new cloud workload inherits, so applications across the carrier start from a consistent, pre-secured foundation rather than bespoke environment builds.

items.name: Monthly Rightsizing Reviews
items.description: Architecture and platform teams review utilization telemetry each month to identify over-provisioned compute, storage, and database tiers. Recommendations are tracked to closure, and persistent low-utilization resources must be downsized, rescheduled, or decommissioned with the application owner's sign-off.

items.name: Multi-AZ Deployment Required for Production
items.description: All production workloads must be deployed across multiple availability zones so that the loss of a single zone does not interrupt service. Single-zone production deployments require a formal exception with a documented risk acceptance from the application owner.

items.name: NSG/Firewall Rules Documented
items.description: All network security group and firewall rules must be documented with their business justification, owner, and review date, and managed as code where supported. Periodic recertification removes stale rules so the effective network policy stays aligned with what is recorded.

items.name: Network Architecture
items.description: Sets the network design rules for cloud environments, minimizing the carrier's exposed surface while keeping connectivity between applications, data platforms, and on-premises systems predictable and inspectable.

items.name: Network Topology
items.description: Landing zones connect to the enterprise network through the standard topology, including approved address space allocation, routing to shared connectivity hubs, and DNS integration. Workload teams consume the pre-built network rather than designing their own connectivity.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Cloud Architecture␟Landing Zone Standards

items.name: No Manual Changes
items.description: Direct changes to cloud resources through portals or CLIs are prohibited in managed environments. Any emergency manual intervention must be back-ported into the code base immediately so the declared state remains the single source of truth.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Cloud Architecture␟Infrastructure as Code

items.name: No Public IPs Except Load Balancers
items.description: Direct public IP assignment to compute resources is prohibited; internet-facing traffic enters only through approved load balancers and application gateways with web application firewall protection. Any other public exposure requires a security-approved exception.

items.name: Policy Guardrails
items.description: Preventive and audit policies are applied to all landing zones at creation, enforcing baseline controls such as allowed regions, encryption requirements, and prohibited services. Guardrails are managed centrally so workload teams operate within compliant boundaries by default.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Cloud Architecture␟Landing Zone Standards

items.name: Private Endpoints
items.description: Platform services such as databases, storage, and messaging must be consumed over private endpoints within the virtual network rather than public service endpoints. This keeps policyholder and claims data off the public internet path even when the service itself is cloud-managed.

items.name: Quarterly DR Testing
items.description: Disaster recovery plans are exercised at least once per quarter, with failover and failback executed against the documented procedure. Test results, gaps, and remediation actions are recorded, and material failures are escalated to the Architecture Review Board and business continuity management.

items.name: RPO/RTO Documented
items.description: Each system records its recovery point objective and recovery time objective, agreed with the owning business area and aligned to its criticality classification. These targets drive the choice of replication, backup, and failover design, and are validated during DR tests.

items.name: Required Tags: Owner, CostCenter, Environment
items.description: Every resource must carry at minimum the Owner, CostCenter, and Environment tags, populated with valid values from the enterprise reference data. These tags underpin cost allocation, incident routing, and lifecycle decisions, and missing or invalid tags are reported for remediation.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Cloud Architecture␟Resource Naming Convention

items.name: Reserved Instances for Steady-State Workloads
items.description: Workloads with stable, predictable demand, such as core policy administration and claims systems, must be covered by reserved instances or savings plans rather than on-demand pricing. Commitment levels are reviewed against the application roadmap so reservations are not purchased for systems slated for retirement or migration.

items.name: Resource Naming Convention
items.description: Standardizes how cloud resources are named and tagged across the enterprise so any engineer, auditor, or cost analyst can identify a resource's purpose, environment, and owner at a glance, and so automation can operate reliably on resource metadata.

items.name: Resource Tagging for Cost Allocation
items.description: Every provisioned cloud resource must carry the mandatory cost-allocation tags so that spend can be charged back to the owning business unit, product line, or transformation initiative. Untagged resources are flagged by policy and remediated within the billing cycle, keeping showback and chargeback reports accurate for P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits workloads.

items.name: Standard Naming Pattern {env}-{region}-{app}-{resource}-{instance}
items.description: Resources are named using the mandated pattern of environment, region, application, resource type, and instance, using the approved abbreviation lists for each segment. The convention is enforced through provisioning policy so non-conforming names are rejected before deployment.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Cloud Architecture␟Resource Naming Convention

items.name: Standard Subscription Structure
items.description: Subscriptions and accounts are organized according to the enterprise hierarchy, separating production from non-production and aligning to business domains and management groups. New subscriptions are vended through the standard process rather than created ad hoc, preserving consistent governance scopes.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Cloud Architecture␟Landing Zone Standards

items.name: Terraform Preferred or Bicep
items.description: Infrastructure definitions must be authored in Terraform as the preferred tool, with Bicep accepted for Azure-native teams. Other provisioning tools require an Architecture Review Board exception, and modules should be drawn from the shared, certified module library where one exists.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Cloud Architecture␟Infrastructure as Code

items.name: All Datasets Registered
items.description: Every production dataset, including warehouse tables, lake assets, and key application extracts, must be registered in the enterprise data catalog before it is consumed by downstream users. Unregistered data sources are not approved for reporting or model development.

items.name: Analytics Architecture
items.description: Defines the reference architecture for the carrier's analytics estate, ensuring actuarial, underwriting, and finance teams work from consistently refined data while retaining the freedom to explore within governed boundaries.

items.name: Automated Discovery Preferred
items.description: Lineage should be harvested automatically from pipelines, SQL, and orchestration metadata wherever tooling permits, with manual documentation reserved for gaps the scanners cannot reach. Manually maintained lineage must identify an owner responsible for keeping it current.

items.name: Automated Profiling
items.description: Datasets are profiled on an automated schedule, with quality rules executed in pipelines rather than through periodic manual checks. New sources are profiled before onboarding so structural surprises are caught ahead of production use.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Data Architecture␟Data Quality Standards

items.name: Business Glossary Linked
items.description: Catalog entries are linked to business glossary terms so technical assets are explained in the carrier's own vocabulary, such as written premium, incurred loss, and in-force policy. Glossary terms are owned by business stewards and changes follow the glossary governance process.

items.name: Conceptual, Logical, and Physical Models Required
items.description: Significant data initiatives must produce models at all three levels of abstraction: a conceptual model agreed with the business, a logical model defining entities and relationships, and a physical model reflecting the implemented schema. Each level is reviewed at the appropriate design gate.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Data Architecture␟Data Modeling Standards

items.name: DQ Scores Published
items.description: Quality scores for governed datasets are published to the data catalog and steward dashboards, making fitness-for-purpose visible to consumers before they build on a dataset. Trends are reviewed by the data governance forum to direct improvement effort.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Data Architecture␟Data Quality Standards

items.name: Data Catalog
items.description: Mandates a complete, searchable inventory of the enterprise's data assets so that users across underwriting, claims, and finance can find, understand, and trust the data they consume, with clear accountability for each asset.

items.name: Data Contracts Enforced
items.description: Interfaces between producing and consuming teams are governed by explicit data contracts specifying schema, semantics, quality expectations, and delivery cadence. Contract changes follow a versioned, communicated process so downstream actuarial and reporting consumers are never broken without notice.

items.name: Data Lineage
items.description: Requires that the movement and transformation of data be traceable from source systems through to reports and models, supporting impact analysis, regulatory inquiries, and confidence in figures presented to management and regulators.

items.name: Data Modeling Standards
items.description: Governs how data structures are designed and documented across projects so that models for policies, claims, customers, and products are consistent, reviewable, and intelligible to teams beyond their original authors.

items.name: Data Quality Standards
items.description: Establishes how data quality is defined, measured, and remediated across the enterprise so that decisions on pricing, reserving, and customer service rest on data whose fitness is known rather than assumed.

items.name: ELT Preferred for Cloud
items.description: On cloud analytics platforms, pipelines should load raw data first and transform within the target platform, exploiting its scalable compute and preserving the unmodified source for reprocessing. Traditional ETL patterns are reserved for cases with a documented justification, such as in-flight masking requirements.

items.name: ERD in Approved Tool
items.description: Entity-relationship diagrams must be authored and maintained in the enterprise-approved modeling tool rather than ad hoc drawing applications, so models remain versioned, shareable, and connected to the metadata repository. Exported snapshots in documents are reference copies only.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Data Architecture␟Data Modeling Standards

items.name: ETL/ELT Standards
items.description: Sets the engineering rules for data movement and transformation pipelines so that feeds between core insurance systems, the analytics platform, and downstream consumers are reliable, restartable, and resilient to change.

items.name: End-to-End Lineage Captured
items.description: Lineage must be recorded from originating systems, such as policy administration and claims platforms, through integration and transformation layers to final consumption in reports, dashboards, and models. Critical regulatory and financial reporting flows are prioritized for full coverage.

items.name: Golden Records for Customer, Policy, Claim, and Product
items.description: Authoritative golden records are maintained for the Customer, Policy, Claim, and Product domains, with defined survivorship rules determining which source attributes win when systems disagree. Consuming applications and analytics draw these entities from the mastered source rather than reconciling them locally.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Data Architecture␟Master Data Management

items.name: Governed Self-Service
items.description: Analysts may build their own datasets and reports within sanctioned workspaces, using cataloged sources and subject to access controls and certification before broad sharing. Self-service content that becomes business-critical must be promoted into managed, supported assets.

items.name: Idempotent Pipelines
items.description: Pipelines must be safe to re-run without producing duplicates or corrupting state, using techniques such as merge logic, deterministic keys, and watermarking. This allows failed loads of policy, claims, or billing data to be replayed during incident recovery without manual cleanup.

items.name: Lineage Published to Catalog
items.description: Captured lineage is published into the enterprise data catalog so analysts and auditors can trace any asset's upstream sources and downstream consumers from a single interface. Lineage views are kept synchronized with pipeline changes through the deployment process.

items.name: MDM Hub for Cross-Domain Resolution
items.description: A central MDM hub performs matching, merging, and identity resolution across source systems and business lines, linking, for example, a household's P&C policies with their life and retirement holdings. Match rules and thresholds are governed, and steward workflows handle records the engine cannot resolve automatically.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Data Architecture␟Master Data Management

items.name: Master Data Management
items.description: Governs how the carrier maintains a single trusted version of its most shared business entities, eliminating the conflicting customer, policy, claim, and product records that arise from operating multiple administration systems across business lines.

items.name: Medallion Architecture (Bronze/Silver/Gold)
items.description: Analytics platforms organize data into Bronze raw, Silver conformed, and Gold consumption layers, with defined quality and transformation expectations at each tier. Consumers such as pricing models and regulatory reports draw from Gold, while data engineering work progresses data through the layers under version control.

items.name: Naming Conventions Enforced
items.description: Entity, attribute, table, and column names follow the published enterprise naming standards, including approved abbreviations and class words. Conformance is checked at model review and through automated schema linting where available, preventing divergent vocabularies across the data estate.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Data Architecture␟Data Modeling Standards

items.name: Quality Rules Defined
items.description: Each critical data element carries documented quality rules covering dimensions such as completeness, validity, accuracy, and timeliness, agreed with the data steward and the consuming business areas. Rules are versioned and traceable to the business requirement they protect.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Data Architecture␟Data Quality Standards

items.name: Remediation SLAs
items.description: Quality defects are triaged by severity and remediated within defined service levels, with breaches of SLA on critical elements escalated to the owning steward and domain leadership. Root-cause fixes at the source system are preferred over repeated downstream cleansing.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Data Architecture␟Data Quality Standards

items.name: Schema Evolution Handled
items.description: Pipelines must tolerate additive source schema changes without failure and detect breaking changes explicitly rather than silently dropping or corrupting fields. Schema change handling behavior is documented per pipeline and validated in testing.

items.name: Searchable Metadata
items.description: Technical and business metadata, including schemas, descriptions, classifications, and quality indicators, must be populated and indexed so users can locate assets by keyword, domain, or term. Sparse or stale metadata is treated as a catalog quality defect and remediated by the steward.

items.name: Semantic Layer for BI
items.description: Business intelligence tools connect through a governed semantic layer that defines certified measures, dimensions, and business logic once, including insurance-specific calculations like loss ratio and earned premium. This prevents divergent metric definitions from appearing across departmental dashboards.

items.name: Stewardship Assigned
items.description: Each cataloged asset has a named data steward and owning domain accountable for its definition, quality, and access decisions. Stewardship assignments are kept current as organizational changes occur, so no critical dataset is left without an accountable party.

items.name: Architecture Diagram Standards
items.description: Standardizes the notation, tooling, and lifecycle of architecture diagrams so that designs are communicated consistently across teams and remain trustworthy as systems evolve.

items.name: Architecture Repository
items.description: Defines where architecture knowledge lives and how it is kept current, giving engineers, auditors, and new joiners one reliable place to find the documented state of the carrier's systems.

items.name: C4 Model (Context, Container, Component, Code)
items.description: Architecture diagrams follow the C4 model, presenting systems at the Context, Container, Component, and where useful Code levels of zoom. Each solution design includes at minimum the Context and Container views so reviewers can see both the business landscape and the deployable structure.

items.name: Confluence for Documentation
items.description: Narrative architecture documentation, including solution designs, decision records, and standards, resides in the enterprise Confluence space using the approved page templates. Documentation scattered in personal drives or email does not count as the system of record.

items.name: Draw.io or LucidChart
items.description: Diagrams are produced in draw.io or LucidChart, the two approved tools, using the shared enterprise shape libraries and templates. Restricting tooling keeps diagrams editable by any architect and avoids stranded artifacts in unsupported formats.

items.name: Git for Diagrams-as-Code
items.description: Diagrams expressed as code, such as PlantUML, Mermaid, or Structurizr definitions, are stored in Git repositories where they can be reviewed, versioned, and rendered in pipelines. This keeps machine-readable architecture artifacts adjacent to the systems they describe.

items.name: Non-Functional Requirements
items.description: Every project must capture its non-functional requirements as a formal deliverable, documenting expectations for performance, scalability, availability, security, and compliance before design is approved. This ensures qualities critical to an insurance carrier, such as regulatory compliance and peak-season resilience, are engineered in from the start rather than discovered as gaps in production.

items.name: Operational Runbooks Required Before Go-Live
items.description: No system enters production without runbooks covering startup and shutdown, health checks, common failure modes, escalation paths, and recovery procedures. Runbook completeness is a gate in the production readiness review.

items.name: PlantUML or Mermaid
items.description: Diagrams are authored in PlantUML or Mermaid text notation rather than drawing tools, so they can be diffed, reviewed in pull requests, and rendered automatically in documentation sites.

items.name: Required for Complex Flows
items.description: Sequence diagrams must be produced for flows involving multiple services, asynchronous messaging, or intricate error handling, such as claims intake spanning core systems, payment, and correspondence platforms. Simple single-service request paths do not require one.

items.name: Reviewed Quarterly
items.description: Each runbook is reviewed at least quarterly by the owning team and updated to reflect architectural, tooling, and procedural changes, with the review date recorded on the document. Runbooks found inaccurate during an incident trigger an immediate out-of-cycle update.

items.name: Runbook Requirements
items.description: Ensures every production system is accompanied by current operational documentation, so support teams can execute routine procedures and respond to incidents without depending on the original build team's tribal knowledge.

items.name: Searchable and Maintained
items.description: Repository content must be organized and labeled so material is discoverable by search, and owners review their pages on a defined cadence to archive or update stale content. Pages without a current owner or review date are flagged during periodic repository hygiene sweeps.

items.name: Sequence Diagrams
items.description: Governs when and how interaction flows are diagrammed, so that multi-system behaviors such as quote-to-bind or first notice of loss are explicitly documented and stay synchronized with the code that implements them.

items.name: Stored in Wiki
items.description: Runbooks are published in the enterprise wiki at the standard location for the owning service, linked from monitoring alerts where possible, and accessible to on-call staff at all hours. Copies held only in local files or chat threads do not meet the standard.

items.name: Stored with Code
items.description: Sequence diagram sources live in the repository of the service whose behavior they describe, and updates accompany the code changes that alter the flow. Keeping the diagram in the same change set prevents documentation from drifting behind the implementation.

items.name: Version Controlled
items.description: Diagram source files are stored under version control alongside or referenced from the owning system's repository, so changes are attributable and earlier states recoverable. Static image exports without an editable, versioned source do not satisfy the standard.

items.name: AKS (Kubernetes) for Container Orchestration
items.description: Production container workloads run on Azure Kubernetes Service clusters provisioned through the enterprise landing zone, inheriting standard policies for networking, identity, and admission control. Teams deploy onto shared or dedicated AKS clusters per the platform team's tenancy model rather than operating their own orchestrators.

items.name: Approved Cloud Platforms
items.description: Defines which public cloud providers the enterprise builds on, concentrating skills, tooling, and security controls on a deliberately narrow footprint rather than allowing each project to choose its own platform.

items.name: Approved Databases
items.description: Specifies the sanctioned database technologies by workload type, so teams pick from a supported, secured set with established backup, licensing, and operational practices instead of proliferating one-off data stores.

items.name: Approved Integration
items.description: Names the sanctioned integration technologies and the role each plays, ensuring connections between modern services, legacy insurance platforms, and digital channels are built on supported patterns rather than point-to-point improvisation.

items.name: Approved Languages
items.description: Constrains application development to a curated set of languages and minimum versions, keeping the carrier's codebase maintainable, securable, and staffable across teams and over the long lifespans typical of insurance systems.

items.name: Approved Messaging
items.description: Directs teams to the sanctioned messaging and event-streaming technologies while managing the retirement of legacy middleware, so asynchronous integration across the carrier converges on a supportable footprint.

items.name: Approved Observability
items.description: Defines the enterprise observability toolchain and the role each product plays, so production health across the application estate is monitored, logged, alerted, and visualized through one coherent stack rather than per-team tool choices.

items.name: Artifactory for Artifacts
items.description: All build artifacts, container images, and third-party dependencies are stored in and resolved from Artifactory, providing a single controlled supply chain with vulnerability scanning and immutable release versions. Pulling dependencies directly from public registries in production builds is prohibited.

items.name: Azure API Management for API Gateway
items.description: All APIs exposed beyond their owning team are published through Azure API Management, which provides the standard policies for authentication, throttling, versioning, and analytics. Direct consumer connections that bypass the gateway are not permitted for shared or external-facing APIs.

items.name: Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions for Pipelines
items.description: Build and deployment pipelines run on Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions, using the shared enterprise pipeline templates that embed security scanning and approval gates. Self-hosted or unsanctioned CI systems are not permitted for code that reaches production.

items.name: Azure Monitor and Dynatrace for APM
items.description: Application performance monitoring is delivered through Azure Monitor for platform-level telemetry and Dynatrace for deep application tracing and dependency mapping. Production services must emit telemetry into this stack, instrumented to the enterprise standard, before go-live.

items.name: Azure Primary, AWS Secondary for Specific Workloads
items.description: Microsoft Azure is the default platform for new workloads, where the enterprise landing zones, identity integration, and operational tooling are most mature. AWS is sanctioned only for the specific workload categories where it is the established or superior fit, as documented in the platform selection guidance.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Technology Stack␟Approved Cloud Platforms

items.name: Azure Service Bus and Kafka for Event Streaming
items.description: Azure Service Bus is the standard for enterprise queuing and pub-sub command-style messaging, while Kafka serves high-volume event streaming such as telematics feeds, claims event propagation, and integration event backbones. Teams select between them based on documented pattern guidance rather than preference.

items.name: CI/CD Tooling
items.description: Standardizes the build and delivery toolchain so every team ships software through the same governed pipelines, with quality and provenance controls applied uniformly from commit to production.

items.name: Container Platforms
items.description: Establishes the standard container runtime, development, and packaging stack so containerized workloads are built and operated the same way across the enterprise, from a developer's laptop to production clusters.

items.name: Docker for Local Development
items.description: Developers use Docker for building and running containers locally, working from the approved base images maintained by the platform team. Local images must be rebuilt from the same Dockerfiles the pipeline uses, keeping development parity with what ships to AKS.

items.name: Exceptions Require ARB Approval
items.description: Use of any other language, or of an approved language below its minimum version, requires a documented exception approved by the Architecture Review Board. Approvals record the justification, scope, and expiry so exceptions are revisited rather than becoming permanent.

items.name: Grafana for Dashboards
items.description: Operational dashboards are built in Grafana against the approved telemetry sources, using shared templates for service health views. Each production service maintains at least a standard golden-signals dashboard accessible to its support team.

items.name: GraphQL for BFF Patterns
items.description: Backend-for-frontend layers serving web and mobile experiences may use GraphQL to aggregate multiple downstream services into channel-shaped queries. GraphQL is scoped to the BFF tier and is not the standard for service-to-service or system-of-record APIs.

items.name: Helm for Packaging
items.description: Kubernetes applications are packaged and released as Helm charts following the enterprise chart conventions for values, secrets references, and resource limits. Charts are versioned and published to the artifact repository so deployments are repeatable across environments.

items.name: Java 17+, Python 3.10+, TypeScript/Node.js 18+, C# .NET 6+
items.description: New development uses Java 17 or later, Python 3.10 or later, TypeScript on Node.js 18 or later, or C# on .NET 6 or later. The version floors ensure supported runtimes with current security patching, and existing systems below these versions carry upgrade plans on their technology roadmaps.

items.name: MongoDB for Document Stores
items.description: Where a document model genuinely fits, such as flexible product configuration or content-style payloads, MongoDB is the approved document database. Teams must justify the document model choice at design review rather than defaulting to it to avoid schema design.

items.name: MuleSoft for Legacy Integration
items.description: Connectivity to legacy estate systems, such as mainframe policy administration and older claims platforms, is implemented through MuleSoft, which encapsulates legacy protocols and data formats behind reusable APIs. New direct couplings to legacy interfaces outside MuleSoft require an exception.

items.name: Multi-Cloud by Exception Only
items.description: Architectures spanning both clouds, or introducing any additional provider, require an explicit Architecture Review Board exception supported by a business case covering the added operational, security, and skills cost. Vendor-imposed hosting, such as a SaaS product running on a particular cloud, is recorded but does not constitute approval for custom multi-cloud builds.
items.parentKey: Enterprise & Solution Architecture␟Technology Stack␟Approved Cloud Platforms

items.name: No New TIBCO Implementations
items.description: No new integrations may be built on TIBCO; the existing estate is in run-down and is replaced opportunistically as connected systems are modernized. Any change to a TIBCO flow must first evaluate migrating that flow to MuleSoft, Service Bus, or Kafka.

items.name: PagerDuty for Alerting
items.description: Actionable alerts route through PagerDuty, where on-call schedules, escalation policies, and acknowledgment tracking are maintained per service. Alert definitions must map to runbook entries so responders know the expected action when paged.

items.name: PostgreSQL and SQL Server for OLTP
items.description: Transactional applications, including policy, billing, and claims services, use PostgreSQL or SQL Server as their system of record. The choice between them follows the application's ecosystem and licensing posture, and both are consumed as managed cloud services rather than self-hosted installs where possible.

items.name: RabbitMQ Deprecated
items.description: RabbitMQ is deprecated for new use, and existing brokers may continue only under a managed migration plan with a target decommission date. Enhancements to RabbitMQ-based integrations should be redirected to the approved platforms wherever feasible.

items.name: Redis for Caching
items.description: Redis is the standard technology for application caching, session state, and similar low-latency lookup needs. It is treated as ephemeral by design, and authoritative data must never reside solely in the cache.

items.name: Snowflake and Databricks for Analytics
items.description: Analytical and data science workloads run on Snowflake or Databricks, which host the governed warehouse and lakehouse layers respectively. Building analytics directly against OLTP databases or standing up alternative warehouse engines requires an architecture exception.

items.name: SonarQube for Quality Gates
items.description: Every pipeline executes SonarQube analysis, and builds must pass the enterprise quality gate covering code coverage, maintainability, and security hotspots before promotion. Gate thresholds are set centrally, and waivers are time-boxed and tracked.

items.name: Splunk for Logs
items.description: Application and infrastructure logs are centralized in Splunk with the standard retention, indexing, and access controls, supporting both operational troubleshooting and the audit retention obligations of a regulated insurer. Logs must follow the structured logging standard and exclude unmasked policyholder PII.

items.name: Callback Verification for Bank Account Changes
items.description: Requests to add or change vendor, claimant, or reinsurer bank account details are never actioned from email alone. Treasury staff verify each change by calling a known contact at an independently confirmed phone number on file, documenting the call before the new instructions take effect. This control is the carrier's primary defense against business email compromise schemes targeting claim and premium disbursements.

items.name: Collections Standards
items.description: Governs how the department pursues and resolves outstanding receivables, from agent balances and reinsurance recoverables to corporate trade debt. Ensures aging balances are surfaced early, escalated consistently, and resolved or written off under controlled authority so receivables remain collectible and accurately stated.

items.name: Dual Approval for Payments Over $10K
items.description: Any disbursement exceeding $10,000, whether check, ACH, or wire, requires two independent approvers within the payment system before release. The preparer may not also approve, and approver lists are reviewed quarterly against the delegation-of-authority matrix to confirm limits remain current.

items.name: Dunning Letters per Schedule
items.description: Past-due accounts receive standardized dunning correspondence on a fixed escalation schedule, with templates and timing approved by Legal and Compliance. For policyholder premium balances, the schedule is coordinated with state-mandated cancellation notice requirements so collection activity never conflicts with regulatory notice periods.

items.name: Invoice Approval Workflow
items.description: Every invoice is routed through the AP system's electronic approval workflow, with approvers determined by cost center and delegation-of-authority limits. Manual or out-of-system approvals are prohibited, and the workflow preserves a timestamped audit trail of who reviewed and approved each invoice before payment.

items.name: Invoice Processing
items.description: Defines the controlled path every vendor invoice follows from receipt to posting, covering approval, matching, and adherence to negotiated terms. Ensures the carrier pays only for goods and services actually ordered and received, at the agreed price and on the agreed timeline.

items.name: Payment Controls
items.description: Establishes the safeguards applied before funds leave the company, focused on high-value disbursements and changes to payee banking details. Protects the carrier against payment fraud, business email compromise, and unauthorized transfers.

items.name: Payment Terms Enforced
items.description: Invoices are scheduled for payment according to the contracted vendor terms, neither paid early without Treasury approval nor allowed to slip past due. AP monitors on-time payment performance and captures early-payment discounts where the discount exceeds the carrier's short-term cost of funds.

items.name: Three-Way Match for PO Items
items.description: Invoices tied to purchase orders must match the PO and the goods-receipt or service-acceptance record on quantity and price before they can post. Mismatches outside tolerance are blocked automatically and routed to procurement and the requesting business unit for resolution rather than overridden by AP staff.

items.name: Weekly Aging Review
items.description: The receivables team reviews the full AR aging each week, covering premium receivables, agent and broker balances, and reinsurance recoverables. Balances crossing 30, 60, and 90 day buckets are flagged with a named owner and next action, and the summarized aging is circulated to the Controller for visibility into deteriorating accounts.

items.name: Write-Off Approval Matrix
items.description: Uncollectible balances may only be written off under a documented authority matrix that ties approval level to dollar amount, from receivables manager through Controller to CFO for the largest items. Each write-off requires evidence of collection effort, and aggregate write-off activity is reported quarterly to support bad-debt reserve adequacy.

items.name: 48-Hour Response to Auditor Requests
items.description: Routine auditor requests and follow-up questions receive a substantive response within two business days. Where the underlying support requires longer to assemble, such as actuarial reserve documentation or investment valuation detail, the owner communicates a committed delivery date within the same 48-hour window.

items.name: Annual Audit Plan Input
items.description: Finance leadership provides a formal risk assessment to internal audit during annual planning, identifying areas of elevated concern such as new accounting standards adoption, system conversions, or processes with recent control changes. This input is documented so the approved plan can be traced back to the risks the department raised.

items.name: External Audit Support
items.description: Sets the department's obligations for supporting the independent financial statement and statutory audits, from evidence delivery through resolution of auditor observations. Ensures the audit proceeds on schedule and that issues raised are not left open across reporting cycles.

items.name: Findings Tracked to Closure
items.description: Control deficiencies, adjustments, and management letter comments raised by the external auditors are logged with an accountable owner, remediation plan, and target date. Progress is reviewed with the Controller monthly and reported to the Audit Committee until each finding is verified closed, with prior-year items confirmed resolved before the next audit cycle begins.

items.name: Internal Audit Coordination
items.description: Defines how Finance & Accounting engages with the internal audit function across the audit lifecycle, from planning input through remediation of issues. Ensures internal audit coverage reflects the department's actual risk profile and that its findings produce timely, verifiable corrective action.

items.name: Management Response Within 30 Days
items.description: When internal audit issues a draft report, the responsible finance manager delivers a written management response within 30 calendar days, either accepting the finding with a remediation plan and date or documenting a substantiated disagreement. Responses are reviewed by the Controller before submission to ensure commitments are realistic and properly resourced.

items.name: PBC List Tracked
items.description: The prepared-by-client request list from the external auditors is loaded into a shared tracker with an assigned owner and due date for every item. The audit liaison reviews status weekly during fieldwork, covering both GAAP and statutory audit requests, so late or stalled items are escalated before they threaten the audit timeline.

items.name: Remediation Tracked
items.description: Agreed remediation actions are entered into the issue-tracking system with owners and due dates, and status is reported at the department's monthly controls meeting. Items may only be closed once internal audit validates the corrective action, and overdue items are escalated to the CFO.

items.name: Annual Budget Calendar
items.description: FP&A publishes a budget calendar before the cycle opens, fixing the dates for assumption setting, business unit submissions, challenge sessions, and final approval. The calendar is sequenced so premium, loss, and expense planning across P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits align with actuarial plan-rate timelines and the Board's year-end approval meeting.

items.name: Budget Process
items.description: Governs the construction of the company's annual operating budget across all business lines and corporate functions. Ensures the budget is built on a common timetable and structure and carries explicit executive endorsement before it becomes the baseline for the plan year.

items.name: Executive Approval Required
items.description: The consolidated budget is presented to the executive committee for formal sign-off, and no business unit budget is considered final until that approval is recorded. Subsequent changes to the approved baseline require the same level of authorization, preserving the integrity of variance reporting throughout the year.

items.name: Forecast Standards
items.description: Establishes the cadence and discipline for the company's financial forecast so leadership always has a current, explained view of expected results. Ensures forecast revisions are timely, forward-looking across a consistent horizon, and supported by clear reasoning for movement against plan.

items.name: Monthly Forecast Update
items.description: The forecast is refreshed every month after the close, incorporating actual results, updated actuarial loss picks, and revised production outlooks from the business units. Each cycle follows a published submission deadline so the consolidated update reaches the CFO before month-end business reviews.

items.name: Rolling Four-Quarter Forecast
items.description: FP&A maintains a forecast that always extends four quarters ahead, crossing fiscal year boundaries rather than truncating at year end. The horizon covers premium production, loss ratios, investment income, and operating expenses by business segment, giving leadership a continuous forward view for capital and reinsurance planning.

items.name: Standardized Templates
items.description: All budget submissions use the templates issued by FP&A, with a common chart-of-accounts mapping, consistent expense allocation drivers, and prescribed assumption fields. This uniformity allows submissions from underwriting, claims, and corporate functions to be consolidated and compared without manual restatement.

items.name: Variance Explanation Required
items.description: Every forecast revision is accompanied by a written explanation of significant movements against both the prior forecast and the annual plan, attributing changes to specific drivers such as catastrophe activity, rate achievement, or expense timing. Unexplained variances above the materiality threshold are returned to the submitting unit before the forecast is accepted.

items.name: Aging of Reconciling Items
items.description: Open reconciling items are individually listed with the date they arose and an explanation, and items aging beyond 60 days are escalated to the assistant controller with a resolution plan. Items that cannot be substantiated within 90 days are assessed for write-off or adjustment rather than carried indefinitely.

items.name: Close Calendar
items.description: Governs the scheduling and monitoring of the monthly and quarterly accounting close so that every contributor works to the same published timetable. Ensures the close completes predictably and that schedule slippage is visible and addressed rather than absorbed silently.

items.name: Close Checklist
items.description: Requires the close to be executed against a controlled, evidenced checklist rather than individual memory or informal routine. Ensures every required close task is completed, accountably signed off, and supported by retained documentation that can withstand audit scrutiny.

items.name: Evidence Retained
items.description: Supporting documentation for each completed checklist task is attached or referenced within the close management tool and retained per the corporate records schedule.
